Making sense out of hemp

By JOHN FLOWERS

ADDISON COUNTY - To Middlebury entrepreneur Netaka White, industrial hemp represents his livelihood, an economically sustainable plant that can be used for everything from fabric to shampoo.

But to area police and Gov. Howard Dean, hemp is cannabis sativa, a botanical relative of marijuana, the legalization of which would complicate drug enforcement and send a bad message to kids.
See

The battle to legalize industrial hemp rages on in Montpelier, with a major front here in Addison County, which was identified in a recent University of Vermont report as the most fertile area in the state in which to grow the crop.

So while top state and federal officials are discounting chances for reintroducing industrial hemp growth in the United States, a vocal contingent of county lawmakers, activists and entrepreneurs continue to lobby fiercely for the crop in Montpelier.

"We’re missing the boat here, economically," said Sen. Elizabeth Ready, D-Addison County, who is a co-sponsor of hemp legalization legislation this year.

"It’s clearly an uphill battle with the government," Ready said.

Ready is a co-sponsor of S.285, a bill which would enable property owners to apply for a license to grow industrial hemp on pre-approved plots. The license would be granted by the commissioner of the Vermont Department of Agriculture and the Drug Enforcement Agency of the United States Department of Justice.

The renewable licenses would be good for two years.

"The fact that we would have some designated sites would mean there would be no back-door approach," Ready said.

"Any other site would simply be illegal."

Ready said S.285 is currently in the Senate Agriculture Committee. She acknowledged there was little chance the bill would be acted upon this year.

"I’ll keep introducing it until it becomes law," Ready said.

Hemp was grown extensively throughout this country during the 19th century and early part of the 20th century. It once was a popular, resilient fabric for making items ranging from boat sails to shoes.

Domestic production of industrial hemp was banned more than a half-century ago, as its kinship with marijuana came more into focus - though it does not contain comparable levels of the chemical THC, which induces the high from smoking pot.

Industrial hemp continues to be grown in some 30 countries throughout the world, including France, Holland and, this year, Canada.

Lawmakers decided to re-examine the viability of hemp as an agricultural crop last year and commissioned a study on the issue by the University of Vermont.

That study, released in January, yielded some of the following findings:

Addison County has 186,012 acres on which hemp could be grown, the most in the state. Chittenden County was second, with 137,367 acres.
The economic impact of growing hemp for a large hemp sector in Vermont would translate into $2.5 million for the state economy and 59 jobs. A small hemp sector operation would yield $67,000 and two jobs.
The tradeoff of the state’s hay crops for hemp crops could be a losing proposition for farmers.

"I think the results were positive, but it didn’t go far enough in exploring the benefit to Vermont," Addison resident John Ball, a hemp researcher and prospective entrepreneur, said of the UVM study.

DIVERSIFICATION

The benefits go beyond economics, Ball noted. While the UVM study shows little economic incentive for a farmer to grow hemp over another cash crop such as corn, Ball said hemp - and its diversity - would make it another weapon in agriculture’s dwindling economic arsenal.

"It’s an alternative product for us," Ball said.

Ball argued that Vermont could, and should, be at the forefront of the hemp movement. In so doing, he said, the state could pave the way for other states and get into "specialty niche" aspects of hemp production - such as seeds.

Ball argued that Vermont could, and should, be at the forefront of the hemp movement. In so doing, he said, the state could pave the way for other states and get into "specialty niche" aspects of hemp production - such as seeds.

"It’s an excellent opportunity," Ball said. "If the infrastructure doesn’t exist... it’s an opportunity for entrepreneurs to get into this business."

Ball and other local hemp proponents are looking to buy a hemp seed press. When and if hemp becomes legal, they would use the press to extract oil, which they said produces two essential fatty acids for the human body. Hemp seed oil is sometimes used in salad dressing and other recipes.

Ball called hemp a "sustainable alternative to petrochemical-based products."

Ball is optimistic that the Legislature will eventually pass a "veto-proof" bill to legalize industrial hemp. The United States, he said, cannot afford to pass on a crop that is widely grown on the worldwide market.

"I see no way that it cannot eventually happen, because of the pressure of outside markets," Ball said. "World markets will dictate."

FARM BUREAU SUPPORT

Last year, the Vermont Farm Bureau actively supported legislation which led to the UVM hemp study. But the Farm Bureau is taking a more passive approach on the issue this year, mainly due to events at last January’s annual American Farm Bureau convention, according to VFB President Clark Hinsdale III.

At that meeting, Hinsdale explained, the American Farm Bureau’s state delegates narrowly voted to reverse their 1997 resolution supporting research into the viability of industrial hemp production. The reversal, Hinsdale said, came after anti-hemp letters were sent to Farm Bureau officials by Barry McCaffrey, President Bill Clinton’s drug czar.

Hinsdale said he voted to uphold the 1997 resolution, but was unsuccessful. Hinsdale was Vermont’s lone delegate to the convention.

"We debated dissenting from national policy, but we chose not to," Hinsdale said. A major reason: the fear of retribution against the fragile Northeast Dairy Compact by anti-hemp delegates from non-dairy states.

"We decided that hemp wasn’t a big enough issue to fall against our sword, as opposed to dairy issues," Hinsdale said.

"We also realized that without policy changes at the national level, it would all be for nought anyway."

Hinsdale said he and other Vermont farmers support hemp research, despite the American Farm Bureau stance. He added that Vermont farmers would not be placed at an economic disadvantage with their Canadian counterparts, who can now begin growing it.

"Agricultural policy in Canada is a huge variable," said Hinsdale. "The hemp issue may be the latest issue where the Canadians are eating our lunch, from an agricultural policy point of view."

If there’s any advantage to the Canadians doing it first, it’s that Vermont and the United States can take some notes on how things work out north of the border.

"If it works, it may break down some of the barriers that exist to hemp production here," Hinsdale said, adding, "I haven’t heard a decent argument yet at the state or national level in not moving ahead to establish a protocol for growing the (hemp)."

Hinsdale believes that hemp will eventually be reintroduced to the United States. While he said hemp would help Vermont farmers diversify their crops, the brightest future for hemp probably lies further west.

"My guess is that if hemp can be done in a big way, it will be grown in the flat, fertile soils of the Midwest," Hinsdale said.

DOES HEMP PAY?

But Vermont Department of Agriculture officials reiterated that it seems economically unlikely that farmers will want to grow hemp in a big way.

Roger Clapp, deputy commissioner for agricultural development for the Vermont Department of Agriculture, has researched the hemp issue for the past several months. His research has revealed, among other things, that hemp is likely to fetch a farmer $150 to $250 per acre. That same acre would generate around $400 in corn production, according to Clapp.

"The way I read the (UVM) report, you can have a greater return per acre for growing corn than hemp and have a lot fewer hurdles to jump over," Clapp said.

Even if the floodgates suddenly opened on hemp production in Vermont, Clapp noted there would be no place to have the substance processed into fabric or other goods. Clapp said he conducted a recent survey of around a dozen major users of industrial hemp, asking them if they would be interested in establishing a processing plant in Vermont if the laws changed.

"The answer from all of them was ‘no,’" Clapp said.

If Vermont farmers want to delve into alternative markets, it will be less difficult and probably more profitable for them to look at such crops as organic wheat, organic oats and soy beans, Clapp noted.

"With limited resources, we are most interested in getting the most immediate return to farmers," Clapp said.

The state is currently looking into a "natural fiber facility" that could help farmers process wool from sheep and llamas, along with other fibers. The facility doesn’t contemplate hemp fiber.

"We seem to be finding better support for fiber other than industrial hemp," Clapp said.

POLICE ROADBLOCK
See

Economics aside, the opposition by state and federal police agencies is yet another strike against hemp, Clapp noted.

"I think that one issue that hasn’t been adequately been dealt with is that we are still dealing with a controlled substance," Clapp said.

Middlebury Police Chief Thomas Hanley summed up the Vermont Association of Chiefs of Police (VACP) position on hemp in a recent letter to Vermont Agriculture Commissioner Leon Graves.

Objections included:

"There is no way to differentiate between leaf and plant material of cannabis sativa cultivated as industrial hemp or marijuana, thereby effectively ending enforcement of possession laws."
"Police have no way to quantify THC content in the field, and hemp product mixed with marijuana product would be indistinguishable and could skew laboratory sampling for THC content."
A new agency would likely have to be created to police cultivation and processing of industrial hemp.

"The VACP opposes the legalization of cannabis sativa in all its forms, including that cultivated as industrial hemp," Hanley stated.

Gov. Howard Dean last month reiterated his firm opposition to hemp, noting its kinship to marijuana. Dean has said that legalizing hemp would be a setback and contradiction to state and national substance abuse efforts.

"The VACP opposes the legalization of cannabis sativa in all its forms, including that cultivated as industrial hemp," Hanley stated.

HEMP ISN’T POT

Hemp proponents, however, claim that comparing hemp to marijuana is inaccurate. Such arguments, they say, have gone up in smoke in the many industrialized Asian and European nations that have legalized the crop.

Proponents argue that anyone who seeks to disguise marijuana in a hemp crop would be foolhardy, as cross-pollination would ruin the pot by reducing its THC content. Smoking hemp, they argue, will not produce a high, but an excruciating headache.

"I don’t believe industrial hemp is a drug; it’s related to a drug," Ready said, adding that attempts to legalize hemp should not be construed as efforts to legalize marijuana.

LOCAL CONNECTION

While politicians, economists and farmers debate the future of hemp, Netaka White of Middlebury is living it. He and his wife Claire Artis opened Greenfields Mercantile on Main Street in Middlebury last year. That store is the retail arm of Artisan Weavers, a commercial manufacturer of hemp travel gear and accessories, also based in Middlebury.

White said his business has been growing at a 50 percent rate annually, requiring Artisan Weavers to recently transplant to more spacious quarters in the Marble Works.

Artisan Weavers will import $250,000 in hemp fabric from Hungary this year, money he wished he were spending in the Vermont and national economies.

"It’s a growing world market," White said. And that market isn’t just for fabric - it’s for paper, hemp seed oil, soaps, shampoos and many other household items.

"There are thousands of gallons of (hemp seed) oil being purchased yearly in this country, and it’s all being imported," White said.

White said with hemp legalized, producers could gradually begin putting the processing infrastructure in place. Prices of hemp clothing and accessories would go down to a point where a pair of hemp jeans would be similar to the cost of a pair of Levis.

"Because of the expensive processing requirement, it will always remain a premium product, like linen," White said.

While the economics of hemp may never see it replace corn or hay in the fields, White agreed that it could provide a formidable value-added crop for farmers.

"A farmer stands to gain more in the long run" with hemp, White said. "They could integrate it as a rotation crop and see how it goes."

White added that he believed police agencies’ misgivings about hemp are ill-founded.

"I would challenge any law enforcement entity to come up with more than an anecdotal instance (of hemp problems)," White said. "The drug issue is being used to keep people off guard, to play on their fears."

Like other hemp proponents, White believes that legalization of the crop is inevitable.

"It is only a matter of time," White said.
